title: VOIAJOR — Voyager 1 and 2, from launch into the far future
desc: A detailed simulation of the trajectories of Voyager 1 and 2, from 1977 to over a billion years from now, at any scale.

ap.note: Literature: NASA/JPL, via Wikipedia. Over light-year distances, an error of a few degrees in a probe's direction of motion changes the minimum distance by tenths of a light-year or more (for Sirius, over two light-years), so the model's values are only indicative.
ab.p1: The paths of the two Voyager probes from 1977 to a future up to 1 billion years away, at any scale: from Earth's orbit to the disk of the Milky Way. The 1 light-day circle (≈173 AU) is the milestone Voyager 1 is heading towards in 2026–2027.
ab.p2: Planets: mean Keplerian orbital elements (JPL, valid 1800–2050). Until 5 Nov 2026: ballistic arcs (heliocentric conics, the Lambert problem) from launch to each planet, on the actual flyby dates; gravity assists appear as sudden changes of speed at the planet. Then a straight line with solar gravitational deceleration, calibrated to reach the position of 5 Nov 2026. After 2026: inertial motion plus the Sun's correction, and over the long term the Galaxy's pull through the epicyclic (Hill) equations with Oort constants A=15.3 and B=−11.9 km/s/kpc and a vertical frequency of ≈0.08 rad/Myr. Stars: J2000 positions, parallax, proper motion and approximate radial velocity, propagated with the same dynamics.
ab.p3: The 2026 positions (distance, direction) are approximations; at light-year scales they differ from JPL ephemerides. No pull from other bodies and no trajectory corrections; planetary flybys are treated as points (patched conics). The galactic model is a linearization around the Sun's orbit: accurate over tens of millions of years, indicative from hundreds of millions of years onward, when the probes are kiloparsecs from the Sun. The dates for the end of transmission are estimates, not official predictions.
ab.p4: On start-up the app syncs with the device clock (“Real time” mode): relative dates (“ago”, “in”) and the “today” marker on the path refer to today. The probes' position is extrapolated from the last calibrated position (5 Nov 2026), valid for any later date; the “Now” button returns to real time at any moment.
ab.p5: The “📅 Date” button opens a window where you can pick an exact calendar date (time in UTC, from the launches to +1 billion years), an interval relative to today (“in 250 years”, “10 years ago”) or a quick moment. After you choose, “Play” continues from there, at 1 year per second. The page address gets a #t= marker that can be saved or sent.
ab.p6: Drag on the screen to rotate, wheel / pinch to zoom (this turns off auto-zoom), double-click to reset the angle. Space = play / pause. The “co-rotating” frame shows the path in the system that rotates with the Galaxy.
ab.p7: Each probe carries a gold-plated copper disc with sounds and images of Earth, as a message for a possible discovery in the very distant future.
ab.src: Mission data source: NASA/JPL. A single-file app that works without internet.

ab.p8: Beyond a few billion years the paths are illustrative: the probes are assumed indestructible (in reality they decay far sooner), the Galaxy evaporates at ≈10¹⁹ years, and cosmic expansion halts the probes a few million ly out. The cosmological events are theoretical estimates, not certainties.
ev.mw.x: The galaxies merge; the probes, drifting in the disc, will almost certainly not hit any star.
ev.rg.t: The Sun becomes a red giant
ev.rg.x: The Sun swells and engulfs Mercury and Venus. The probes are far away in interstellar space and feel nothing.
ev.wd.t: The Sun becomes a white dwarf
ev.wd.x: The Sun sheds its outer layers and is left as a small, hot core that cools slowly.
ev.lg.t: The Local Group becomes a single galaxy
ev.lg.x: The rest of the Universe recedes beyond the horizon; the night sky is left with one giant galaxy.
ev.sf.x: The gas is used up; no new stars form, only the existing ones keep burning.
ev.ls.x: The red dwarfs burn out. The sky turns completely black: no star lights the Galaxy any more.
ev.bd.t: Planets break free of their stars
ev.bd.x: Close encounters tear planets away from the stellar remnants; only cold, wandering bodies remain.
ev.ge.x: Gravitational encounters fling the stellar remnants outward. In this illustration the probes are ejected and set off alone into the void.
ev.pd.x: If protons decay, all ordinary matter gradually vanishes. The probes survive only by our assumption.
ev.bh1.x: Hawking radiation consumes them; only photons and sparse particles remain, ever more spread out.
ev.bh2.x: End of the simulation: an almost empty Universe whose only relic is — by assumption — Voyager.
tour.1.x: In August and September 1977 Voyager 2 and then Voyager 1 leave Cape Canaveral, using a planetary alignment that comes once in ~175 years.
tour.2.x: Voyager 1 passes Jupiter on 5 March 1979 and finds active volcanoes on Io and the planet’s rings. Jupiter’s gravity flings it on towards Saturn.
tour.3.x: On 12 November 1980 Voyager 1 studies Saturn and Titan. The close pass of Titan throws it above the plane of the planets: from here on it sees no more planets.
tour.4.x: Voyager 2 carries on and reaches Neptune on 25 August 1989: the only probe ever to have visited Uranus and Neptune.
tour.5.x: On 14 February 1990 Voyager 1 turns back and photographs Earth from ~6 billion km: a single pixel lost in a beam of light.
tour.6.x: On 25 August 2012 Voyager 1 becomes the first human-made object in interstellar space, where the solar wind no longer dominates.
tour.7.x: Voyager 1 is {0} from the Sun — its signal needs {1} to reach us. Voyager 2 is at {2}.
tour.8.x: On 18 November 2026 Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth — the first time a radio signal needs 24 hours one way. Press “Send a radio signal” in the data panel.
tour.9.x: In a few centuries the probes enter the Oort cloud: a swarm of comets around the Sun that takes ~300 years just to reach its inner edge.
tour.10.x: In ~40,000 years Voyager 1 passes 1.6 ly from Gliese 445 and Voyager 2 passes 1.7 ly from Ross 248. The probes will not “visit” them, only drift by.
tour.11.x: In half a billion years the probes complete about a third of a lap of the Galaxy. The surrounding stars change entirely; the Sun is no longer visible to the naked eye.
tour.12.x: In ~4.5 billion years the Milky Way and Andromeda collide. The gaps between stars are so vast that almost no star hits another.
tour.13.x: The Sun becomes a red giant, then a white dwarf. The inner planets are lost, but the Voyagers, far away, go on undisturbed.
tour.14.x: After ~100 trillion years the last stars go out. The dark Universe has no light of its own: the probes fly through total night.
tour.15.x: At ~10¹⁹ years the Galaxy evaporates and the probes are flung out of it. The journey into the intergalactic void begins, at the slow speed of a fossil.
tour.16.x: By 10¹⁰⁰ years even the last black holes are gone. Here the simulation ends — and, by assumption, Voyager remains the last messenger of a world that once was.
